description: CF SGO 25 is an interdisciplinary team from Santiago del Estero, Argentina, with backgrounds in political science, public policy, data-driven management, and medicine.  Our team combines research, policy analysis, project coordination, communication, and health knowledge, and we are especially interested in challenges related to health, agriculture, Earth observation, and public impact.
summary:
SANTIAGRO is an agricultural assistance platform for small and medium-sized farmers in Santiago del Estero, Argentina. It combines Meteomatics weather data with soil information and each plot's history to generate preliminary reports, assess crop rotation and guide production decisions, supported by a virtual assistant: MIA (Mi Inteligencia Agrícola, "My Agricultural Intelligence").
Small and medium-sized farmers struggle to plan resilient crop rotations because climate, satellite and agricultural information is scattered.
SANTIAGRO lets farmers record each plot's location, area, sowing date, crop, and soil moisture, texture and salinity, and enter the crops of the previous, current and next seasons. Using this data and local weather, the platform flags risks and missing data, detects repetitions and lack of diversity in the crop sequence, and assesses the planned rotation, promoting more sustainable soil use, preserving soil fertility and improving production planning.
The prototype already integrates Meteomatics (forecasts) and NASA POWER (official historical climate data). The next stage will add Planetary Computer (vegetation cover and plot evolution from satellite imagery), Google Maps (location of farms and plots) and Firebase (farmer profile and history). The website was developed with the assistance of Claude.
details:
What exactly does it do?

SANTIAGRO is a digital agricultural assistance platform built around a decision-support module for crop rotation, designed for small and medium-sized farmers across the productive localities of Santiago del Estero, Argentina.

Farmers can record each plot’s location, area, sowing date, crop, and soil moisture, texture and salinity, and enter the crops of the previous, current and next seasons. With this data, the platform analyzes the crop sequence, identifies repetitions and lack of diversity, and assesses the planned rotation. The goal is to promote more sustainable soil use, preserve soil fertility and improve production planning.

The prototype integrates Meteomatics weather data (rainfall, temperature, humidity and wind) for forecasts and current conditions, and NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources) as an official source of historical agroclimatic data. NASA POWER already covers eleven productive localities of the province and lets farmers compare them side by side. It provides temperature and rainfall context for the farmer’s selected locality. The next stage will add three more sources: Planetary Computer for vegetation cover and plot evolution from satellite imagery, Google Maps to locate farms and plots, and Firebase for farmer profiles and history. SANTIAGRO also includes MIA (Mi Inteligencia Agrícola, “My Agricultural Intelligence”), a virtual assistant that helps farmers ask questions and understand the information.

How does it work?

The farmer enters the plot’s data and gets a preliminary report. The report shows favorable factors, risks, missing data and a risk indicator. In the rotation module, the farmer enters the crops of each plot by season. The platform then flags repetitions, whether grasses and legumes alternate, and whether cover crops are included.

The report is complemented with the area’s weather, so decisions take local environmental conditions into account. It also includes a “Historical climate context – NASA POWER” section, with mean and maximum temperature, accumulated rainfall and days above 35 °C from NASA data for the selected locality, and compares the forecast with the same calendar days of previous years where forecast data is available. MIA answers questions and helps farmers understand the reports. SANTIAGRO does not replace an agronomist; it organizes the information so the consultation with one is more precise.

What are the benefits?

Makes crop rotation planning easier, based on what was sown in each plot.

Promotes soil fertility conservation and the sustainable use of natural resources.

Helps reduce the risks of poor planning by also showing which data is missing.

Combines weather, NASA historical climate data, soil and production information in a single report.

Brings technological tools and technical knowledge to small and medium-sized farmers throughout the province.
